See ibid., where the hadith is quoted on the authority of ’Abdallah ibn Mas’ûd. There are, however, many variations in the number of figures making up this mystical hierarchy. Rûzbehân seems to have given his fullest account in the long prologue to his Persian book on the Paradoxes of the Sufis (pp. 52–53 of our edition, cited above, p. 15, note 6). This gives us some sense of the importance of the symbolic visions in which the young Rûzbehân began to realize that he himself was one of the Awliyâ’ (friends of God). On the same page of the Ighâna, Rûzbehân also reports another tradition from Shaykh Abû Bakr al-Kattânî: 300 Noqabâ’ residing in the West, 70 Nojabâ’ residing in the East, 40 Bodalâ’ (= Abdâl), seven Abhyâr who are continually travelling, three ’Omadâ’, and finally the Pole (Ghawth), in Mecca. There is also mention of the 124,000 Walis corresponding to the 124,000 prophets. The structure of their hierarchy mirrors the configurations of the stars: the same imago mundi, or image of the world, is embodied in both. The key to this conception very probably lies in Central Asian Sufism, while the source of its astronomical symbolism—with the special prominence of Ursa Major—may be sought in Taoist and Buddhist cosmologies. This hierarchy remains a living idea in Shiism today, notably in the Shaykhi school, where it sustains the conception of a purely spiritual Church, an Ecclesia spiritualis. It differs, however, from the hierarchy of Sunni Sufism by reserving walâyat (spiritual guardianship) to the holy Imams alone. Beneath them, the Noqabâ’ and Nojabâ’ are mirrors (mazâhir) of the Imam. This esoteric hierarchy has already been mentioned here (vol. I, Chapter III, § 4); see also below, vol. IV, Books VI and VII. Bringing together the different traditions on this subject would take an entire book. See L’Homme de lumière, index. ↩

The Kitâb al-Ighâna discusses this subject twice: the hierarchy of the Invisible Ones, whom Rûzbehân regards as exceptionally important, because they are the eyes through which our world remains a world upon which God gazes. First (fols. 14a–b), Rûzbehân gives his own account. Then (fols. 15a–b) he returns to the subject through a conversation between ’Alî ibn Mohammad Daylamî and his master, ’Abdallah Mohammad ibn Khaffî, whom Rûzbehân credits with treating the matter more beautifully, elegantly, and clearly than he himself had done. This same figure wrote one of the earliest mystical treatises on the experience of love (Kitâb ’atf al-alif; see our Introduction au Jasmin, p. 15 and note 23). ↩

The traditional distinction between the attributes of Majesty (jalâl) and Beauty or Grace (jamâl) is borne out by Rûzbehân’s account of his own experience, his Diarium. See below, p. 49, note 35, on the vision “in the most beautiful of forms.” The attributes of Jalâl and Jamâl correspond respectively to the fourth and fifth sefirot in Jewish Kabbalah: Gebura and Hesed. ↩

Af’âl: divine activities or operations, each of which manifests a divine Attribute in a form suited to the nature of the person to whom it appears. See below, Book IV, Chapter III, § 7 (the precedence given to “maternal lines” or “lines of Eve” among the Hurufis). It is because of this precedence that God shows his face to the Prophet with these features, in a vision on which the Sufis meditate tirelessly; see below, p. 49, note 35. ↩

Jalâl and Jamâl: see above, p. 46, note 30. We should also think here of Rudolf Otto’s categories, tremendum and fascinans, with all the qualifications required by the different forms taken by the sacred. In one sense, they may be translated, as Fritz Meier does (op. cit.), by Erhabenheit (sublimity) and Freundlichkeit (kindliness). Yet these are merely aspects and consequences flowing from the primordial Image. Better to keep the primary meanings: Majesty (awe-inspiring severity) and Beauty (which fascinates). Otherwise, we break the unity of the language characteristic of this mystical worship of Beauty (jamâl-parastî), and lose sight of the fact that the primordial Image presses itself upon the visionary as an entirely specific, visible form (see the following note). ↩

These are the characteristic words of the famous “hadith of the vision,” in which the Prophet declares: “I saw my Lord in the most beautiful of forms, as a youth with abundant hair, seated upon the Throne of grace. He wore a green robe, with a golden headdress upon his hair and golden sandals upon his feet.” On this hadith, its variants, and its use as a theme of meditation, see our Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, pp. 203 ff.; above, pp. 46 and 48, notes 30 and 34; and below, p. 93, notes 112 and 114. In Rûzbehân’s time, even within Iran, Central Asian Turkic beauty was regarded as the ideal of beauty, among both young women and young male pages. Rûzbehân’s visions and his vocabulary both bear its imprint. Perhaps a link should be drawn between the extraordinary beauty for which the inhabitants of certain towns in what is now Turkestan were renowned and the testimony of Abû Shakûr Sâlimî (5th/10th century), according to whom the Manichaeans of Central Asia distinguished themselves by their reverence for every beautiful being. See our Introduction au Jasmin, pp. 100 ff. This makes it clear why, when the occasion arises, it would be quite impossible to translate the expression simply as “young Turks”! See below, notes 40, 44–45, and 49, and our study Manichéisme et religion de la beauté, in Cahiers du Sud, April 1963. ↩

Hazrat al-Haqq: on the idea of Hazrat (“presence,” a plane of consciousness, degree of being, or “dignity,” as Raymond Lull translated it), see our Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, pp. 167 ff., 262–263. Red light is a dominant feature of Rûzbehân’s visions. Compare this other vision: “One night I saw something enveloping the Heavens. It was a glittering red light. I asked: What is that? Michael, as the universal divine Soul, the lower right-hand pillar of the Throne and the highest summit of the Malakût (spiritual kingdom), is red. In Iranian Shiism of the preceding century, one of the leaders of the Shaykhi school, Shaykh Mohammad Karîm Khân Kermânî (whose brilliant work is vast almost beyond reckoning; see below, vol. IV, Book VI, Chapter II), wrote, among other things, an entire treatise on red light, ranging from the optical phenomenon to the colour’s esoteric meaning (Risâlat al-yâqûtat al-hamrâ’). We see no reason to doubt the authenticity of this anecdote. Rûzbehân’s stay in Mecca is firmly attested by our sources, among them the biography written by his great-grandson, Shaykh Sharafoddîn Ibrahim, son of Rûzbehân II, and is confirmed by the setting of several of his visions. As for its psychological credibility, his experience in Mecca accords with the whole teaching of the Jasmin. It was certainly not some sordid, commonplace adventure—an episode in which he “threw off his monk’s habit.” His purity matched the sincerity that Ibn ’Arabî recognizes in him. Rûzbehân remained faithful to the teaching of the famous hadith: “Whoever loves, remains chaste, and dies without betraying his secret, dies as a truthful Witness.” His conduct was that of a true “faithful lover”: the young woman whose beauty had awakened his love knew nothing of it until others told her. See Introduction au Jasmin, pp. 108–111. Compare the answer Rûzbehân gave Emir Sa’d of Shiraz, preserved in a long poem by Fakhroddîn ’Erâqî: “Before Abraham the fire bloomed harmlessly like a rose, and Moses’ body was not consumed by the theophany of the Burning Bush. To your eyes my contemplation may seem sensual; but what is born of my heart’s inclination is purely spiritual.” See ibid., p. 110, note 149. ↩

Ibn ’Arabî first came to Mecca in AD 1201. By then, Rûzbehân had long been settled in Shiraz, where he died in 1209. His own stay in Mecca must have occurred long enough before Ibn ’Arabî’s visit for the anecdote to have become well known among the Sufis, but recently enough for everyone still to remember it. There is no reason to transfer the story to his namesake Rûzbehân Kazrûnî Misrî, from whom he must be carefully distinguished, and who was the master of Najm Kobrâ. The contemplative gaze (nazar) that takes the beloved’s beauty as its witness of contemplation (shâhid) is a gaze that transforms. Someone who knows they are being transformed in this way comes into the truth of their inner beauty: they see themselves as they are seen by the one who contemplates them. “When these beautiful beings are favoured by the mystical contemplation of the Sufis and purify their inward being, the light of their outward beauty passes into their inward being, and their beauty becomes eternal. Otherwise, as they grow older, the light of their outward beauty gradually fades through the accidents of nature. No longer held in the contemplative gaze of the mystics, their being is invaded by Darkness” (Jasmin, Chapter VII, § 103). ↩

Jasmin, §§ 16–17, p. 118. Rûzbehân also says: “The place—that is, the material, visible human form—which I call the city of God is indeed the place of the soul, yet it does not contain the soul.” ↩

Jasmin, § 18, p. 119. For Rûzbehân, this is certainly not a matter of reasoning from the beauty of a creature to the beauty of the Creator as its cause; it is a matter of seeing the Creator’s beauty in the creature itself, because the creature is its only mirror, its unique manifestation. The theophanic vision is immediate and has nothing to do with reasoning via eminentiae, by ascending from finite perfections to a higher, divine perfection. See also below on the shâhid, the “witness of contemplation.” ↩

Jasmin, §§ 19–20, pp. 120–121. Rûzbehân returns to this saying of Zûl-Nûn (Dhu’l-Nûn) Misrî in the chapter devoted to him in his great Commentary on the Paradoxes of the Sufis: “Whoever has become familiar with God becomes familiar with everything beautiful: every gracious face, every pleasing voice, every sweet fragrance.” See pp. 150 ff. of our edition. ↩

See above, Chapter III, on the idea of the shâhid, the witness of contemplation, arising within the divine mystery itself: the Divine Being longs for a Witness to contemplate him, yet can be contemplated by no one other than himself. His longing is only stilled when the one who contemplates him (shâhid) is, in the very act of contemplation, also his own Contemplated (mashhûd), one with himself. The French expression quelqu’un que Dieu regarde (“someone whom God looks at,” as opposed to someone for whom “it is none of his concern”) has a double sense—regarder means both “to look at” and “to concern”—which can suggest this simultaneity. ↩
See Hellmut Ritter, Das Meer der Seele, Leiden, 1956, pp. 47 ff. ↩

Notice the character of this contemplation. Ahmad Ghazâlî places the “obstacle” of a rose between himself and his witness of contemplation. Rûzbehân, while the candle flame rises straight from the candle firmly set in its holder, contemplates the beloved’s beautiful face as he listens to beautiful poetry (Jasmin, §§ 200–201). But he also knows that, to rediscover the secret of the uncreated within a creature in this way, the “daring adventurers of tawhîd” must first have travelled the Path of Trial, crossing the bridge suspended above the hell of sensual nature (see Introduction, p. 18). ↩

Rendering shâhid as “witness of contemplation” suggests a correspondence that comparative study might find between it and the process by which the Dhyânibuddhas, or “Buddhas of contemplation,” come into being. Earlier in this volume (Book I, Chapter VII, § 4), we also discussed the Imam as a Witness of Contemplation. ↩

Gloss 68: wa be-sifat-e Adam bar-amadeh. Compare Jasmin, Chapter V, § 97: “Even before the worlds and their unfolding came into existence, the Divine Being was himself love, lover, and beloved. When the forms and figures that are so many theophanies (ashkâl-e f’il) appeared in the gallery of images belonging to the creative Command, the form of Adam was the quintessence of Being and of beings, because it was the most subtle of the substances of the angelic pleroma (malakût). It was God himself who had put on the garment of Being, and whose Attributes were no longer veiled from the world.” Compare the opening of Suhrawardî’s Vade-mecum of the Faithful in Love. ↩

Jasmin, Chapter VII, §§ 98–101, interpreting the famous “Verse of Light” (Âyat al-Nûr, Qur’an 24:35) as an image of the veils of theophanies. Compare Gloss 69: “The primordial theophany must necessarily take place in the First Intelligence (the Nous), under the attributes of grace and beauty. The Intelligence then reveals itself in the Spirit, the Spirit in the Heart, and from the Niche of the Heart its light is cast into the world of Nature. As for the substance called Intelligence, it receives its beauty directly from the Being of God; consequently, it is itself the cause of the world’s existence (as a manifestation of divine Beauty). It is also the Guide who leads to discovery, to gnostic knowledge, to the lifting of the veil of created existence before the Face of true Reality.” Intelligence, Spirit, Heart: compare Suhrawardî’s triad of Beauty, Love, and Sorrow (here, Book II, Chapter VII, § 3). ↩

Jasmin, Chapter V, § 60. Compare §§ 66–67: the divine Attributes “enter” (dar-âmad) the human form, but only as an image “enters” a mirror. The unity of mirror and reflected image has nothing in common with the disturbance, change, and “constriction” associated with an Incarnation (be-surat-e holûl). Adam is clothed in the lights of uncreated Beauty (jamâl-e qidam). This clothing necessarily involves an ambiguity of appearance (iltibâs), a dokesis or seeming; without it, Adam could not possess the transparency of a mirror. It is this theophany in the person of Adam, on the plane of paradisal humanity, that the Prophet Muhammad recognized, and this is why he proclaimed the religion of love. When he said, “God created Adam as the image of his own form,” he was echoing the verse revealed to him: “I breathed my Spirit into him” (38:72 and 75). “From his person, original Beauty presents itself again in his descendants until the hour of Resurrection”—as a recurring theophany (tajallî), not as an incarnatio continuata, or continuing incarnation. See also Chapter I, § 10. ↩
Jasmin, Chapter X, § 121; see also below, notes 122 and 135. ↩

Gloss 151. It is significant that the prophetic meaning of Beauty inherent in this religion of love leads the Sufi to speak in its characteristic “closed language,” transforming expressions borrowed from the old Zoroastrian religion into symbols of the religion of love. See also below, p. 103, note 137, and earlier, Book II, Chapter VII, § 3, at the end. ↩

Muslim writers on heresy were not “historians of doctrine” (see also below, p. 111, note 147). Although they could distinguish Melkites, Jacobites, and Nestorians, their accounts of the Christologies attributed to these groups lacked technical precision. They did not have enough information to grapple with the difficulties of ittihâd (unio, union) and holûl (enoikesis, indwelling), or to distinguish technically between docetic Christology, monophysite Christology, and the Christology of the Councils. They used the term holûl on every occasion (for examples, see H. Ritter, Das Meer der Seele, pp. 449 ff.). That is why we have just seen Rûzbehân and his commentator vigorously reject the notion of holûl. Their opponents could all the more easily accuse them of it because the relation Rûzbehân understood as that between mirror and image counted, in his opponents’ eyes, as holûl. The misunderstanding seems impossible to dispel. These heresiographers were adept—and for good reason—at recognizing the recurrence of a Christological pattern in every Shia teaching concerning the Imams. Their mistake, which we must avoid, was failing to recognize which Christology was involved. Without that distinction, one is liable to make the gravest errors in speaking of the “divinity of the Imams.” ↩
On this theme, see above, p. 13, note 4, and p. 23, note 15. ↩

According to the episode in the Vita Adae et Evae, §§ 12 ff., and the Gospel of Bartholomew, § 52, which provides the prototype for the Qur’anic account (2:32, 18:48). But this is a prologue taking place “in Heaven.” To interpret it as the outcome of a conflict between Man and the Angels would overlook the fact that Adam—as Rûzbehân has insisted (above, p. 84, note 86; Jasmin, § 97)—was the heavenly Adam, “the purest substance of the angelic world (malakût),” the Angel Adam. ↩

Jasmin, Chapter V, § 75. The beauty of the heavenly Adam is “the Kaaba of the divine attribute of beauty.” To deny that they correspond to one another (Iblîs’s refusal) is to fall into ta’til: to “depose” God, reducing him to an abstraction. ↩

Ibid., § 76: “The subtler a being’s constitution, the more refined its body and noble its soul, and the more transparent its dwelling (its ‘temple,’ haykal) becomes to the substances of primordial light. All the things we admire for their beauty receive an influx of this First Beauty, for every atom of being possesses a soul that comes to it from the divine Operation (fi’l-e Haqq; see above, p. 47, note 31). This soul governs it in accordance with the corresponding Attribute and the theophany of the Essence, and this is especially true of the things we admire for their beauty. Only the eye whose very seeing is certainty can truly see. The nearer one draws to the source of Beauty, the nearer one draws to the covenant of love.” ↩
Ibid., § 63. Compare the context in which Ibn ’Arabî places the same hadith, in Soufisme d’Ibn ’Arabî, pp. 113 ff. ↩

Ibid., § 49. The prophetic meaning of beauty, and thus also the ambiguity of its appearance (iltibâs); the theophanic function that the lover confers upon the beautiful person; that person’s power to lead the lover back to the archetypal source—all these “articles of faith” of the religion of beauty (jamâl-parastî) rest on the primary premise that love existed before creation. “The force that moves (moharrik) the lover is a pre-eternal love (’ishq azalî).” See below, Chapter VI, § 4, where the Platonic and prophetic themes meet, in the texts referred to in note 142. ↩

Ibid., § 50: the elevation of the shâhid (witness) to the rank of shahîd (“martyr”). Compare Mogholta’l’s book “in memory of those faithful in love who have borne true Witness” (ed. O. Spies, Bonner Orient. Stud., 18, 1936). Yet, as we have already stressed, the literal death from love suffered by the heroes of ’odhrîte love gives way here to a mystical meaning. The elevation of the shâhid to shahîd signifies attainment of the esoteric tawhîd: the oneness of lover and beloved, of Contemplator (shâhid) and Contemplated (mashhûd).
